formula_references.source_sentence: To more formally introduce eigenvalues and eigenvectors, suppose, for a square matrix A, that the vector y satisfies the matrix equation for some scalar value, λ. Geometrically, this means that the new vector resulting from transformation of y by A points in the same direction as y (or is exactly reflected about the origin if λ < 0). For such vectors, the only action of the matrix transformation is to scale them by some amount, λ. These vectors thus represent the inherent axes associated with the transformation given by A, and the set of all such vectors, along with their corresponding scalar multipliers, completely describes the geometry of this transformation. Vectors that satisfy Equation A5.6 are referred to as eigenvectors, and their associated scaling factors are eigenvalues, and together they jointly describe the eigenstructure (the intrinsic geometry) of the square matrix, A. If y is an eigenvector, then ay is also an eigenvector, as $ \mathbf{A}(ay) = a(\mathbf{Ay}) = \lambda(ay) $. Note, however, that the associated eigenvalue, λ, remains unchanged. Hence, we typically scale eigenvectors to be of unit length to yield unit or normalized eigenvectors. In particular, if $ y_i $ is any eigenvector associated with the ith eigenvalue, then the associated normalized eigenvector is $ e_i = y_i / \|y_i\| $.
